transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-25
Start time: 14:00 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Recorded: yes (auto)
Attendees: Sara Kim (Redwood AE), Miguel Ortega (Redwood SE), Tess Nguyen (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (Glenwood Cloud Architect), Mark Donnelly (Head of ML), Liam O'Connor (Network Engineer), Ellen Park (Security)

--- Summary (auto) ---
Redwood team walked through private deployment topologies. Glenwood emphasized EU residency, central transit gateway, and strict egress controls. Main questions: do we support PrivateLink/private endpoints in multiple regions, how routing works with transit gateway, certificate and DNS handling for private endpoints, and what the fallbacks are for cross-region traffic.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Sara Kim: Hi everyone, thanks for taking the time. I think we have about 50 minutes, quick intros?
[00:06] Priya Shah: Yeah hi I'm Priya, cloud architect at Glenwood. We're evaluating options for running inference—thinking Redwood Private but need clarity on networking and regions.
[00:12] Mark Donnelly: Mark here, ML lead. Our main ask is predictable latency for inference so customer facing features don't degrade.
[00:16] Miguel Ortega: Great. Quick note — from a topology standpoint Redwood supports three flavors: hosted, dedicated reserved capacity, and private deployments which we can do via VPC peering, PrivateLink/private endpoints, or a transit gateway integration depending on your architecture.
[00:30] Liam O'Connor: Quick clarifying Q — we have a central transit gateway in our EU-central region and then multiple spoke VPCs across EU and US. We need to keep data in EU for PII workloads. How do you see cross-region routing working?
[00:46] Tess Nguyen: Good question. For Private deployments we typically recommend placing Redwood nodes in the region where data residency is required and then peer that VPC to your spoke via peering or TGW. If you need multi-region active/active we can provision endpoints in each region — but you'll want to control routing to ensure EU traffic stays in EU.
[01:05] Priya Shah: So if we use VPC peering, does that mean we have to manage route propagation per spoke? Our infra team tries to limit manual route edits.
[01:13] Miguel Ortega: With peering you'd manage route tables on the spoke. If you want a more centralized approach and avoid sprawl we can support TGW attachments. We have customers who use TGW and then use route policies to keep egress inside region. There are tradeoffs though — TGW can add cost and a single point that needs extra testing for throughput.
[01:30] Liam O'Connor: Also, egress IPs — we require a small set of static egress IPs for allowlisting to third-party data stores. Can Redwood provide static egress IPs for private deployments?
[01:40] Sara Kim: We can. For Private with dedicated egress we can allocate NATs or egress gateways with static IPs, or we can publish a small prefix range per region for allowlist. We'll flag that in the runbook.
[01:51] Ellen Park: Security question — how are audit logs and request-level tracing surfaced? We need logs for PCI/SOC type audits plus SSO integration.
[01:59] Miguel Ortega: We stream audit logs to your S3 or GCS bucket, and we support pushing logs to SIEM via syslog. SSO is SAML/OIDC and RBAC is configurable; we also support KMS integrations for customer-managed keys in Private deployments.
[02:12] Mark Donnelly: On the latency front — what's your typical P95? Our SLA target is p95 under 200ms for 8k context prompts.
[02:20] Tess Nguyen: For models and setup like that we usually see p95 in the 80–180ms range on dedicated hardware in-region, depends on batching, tokenization size and KV cache warm state. We'll need to run a benchmark with your exact prompt mix to be precise.
[02:35] Priya Shah: About DNS — we use split-horizon DNS internally. If we create private endpoints, how do clients resolve the Redwood endpoints?
[02:43] Miguel Ortega: We support private endpoints with customer-provided DNS entries. Typically you create a private hosted zone per region and we publish CNAMEs or you can override with A records pointing to the private interface. Some transcription: sometimes called private-link, private endpoints, PrivateLink — same kind of idea.
[02:58] Liam O'Connor: Are the endpoints interface endpoints (ENI) or is it just routing-based peering?
[03:04] Tess Nguyen: We can do both. Interface endpoints (PrivateLink) give you interface ENIs in your VPC which you can sec-group lock down. Peering gives you direct routing between VPCs but no ENI to attach SGs to. Both are supported; choice depends on your security posture.
[03:19] Priya Shah: We also have regulatory requirement: all inference outputs for EU PII must not leave EU region even if called from US app. Is regional pinning config possible?
[03:29] Miguel Ortega: Yes, we can pin models and routes per tenant or per API key so requests for EU datasets are routed to EU-hosted nodes. That's part of the deployment config for Private.
[03:36] Mark Donnelly: What about fallback logic? If EU cluster hits capacity, do you have auto-fallback to non-EU or spill to hosted? That's a dealbreaker if it leaks PII.
[03:45] Sara Kim: We do not automatically spill PII across regions. Fallbacks can be configured to go to a compatible model in the same region or to fail open depending on your policy. We can implement explicit routing rules and capacity alarms so infra can scale before it starts rejecting requests.
[03:58] Liam O'Connor: Any limits on the number of peering connections or ENIs per endpoint we should consider?
[04:04] Miguel Ortega: AWS-specific limits apply — ENIs per AZ and TGW attachments per account — we document those in our network guide. We also recommend using shared services VPCs or service mesh patterns if you have lots of spokes.
[04:16] Priya Shah: How about cross-account peering? We want Redwood nodes in a dedicated AWS account for isolation.
[04:23] Tess Nguyen: That's common. We can deploy in your account or in a Redwood-managed account with cross-account peering. If in Redwood account we'll require a peering request and you manage the route acceptance. For Private we often push for customer-managed accounts for compliance, but we can be flexible.
[04:39] Mark Donnelly: Pricing — ballpark delta between Dedicated and Private? If we host in our account it changes cost profile right?
[04:46] Sara Kim: Yes. Dedicated is reserved capacity on Redwood-managed infra and is predictable monthly. Private in your VPC will be priced differently — there is a platform fee plus infra consumption. We'll run a cost model once you share the expected QPS, tokens/req, and retention settings.
[05:00] Priya Shah: On certificates and mTLS — can we require mTLS for endpoints?
[05:05] Miguel Ortega: We support client cert auth and mutual TLS for Private endpoints. We also support TLS termination in your VPC if you want to manage certs there.
[05:12] Ellen Park: For audit the timeline — do you have SOC2 type attestation we can ship to procurement?
[05:16] Sara Kim: Yes, SOC2 Type II and ISO27001 artifacts are available; I'll send the package after the call.
[05:22] Liam O'Connor: Two network-specific gotchas we've seen: 1) asymmetric routing when you have NAT in front of TGW, 2) MTU issues when ENIs + encapsulation occur. Do you test for those?
[05:33] Miguel Ortega: We include a network checklist in the onboarding runbook and we recommend an initial lab test where we run synthetic traffic to validate MTU and routing. We'll include recommended MTU settings.
[05:43] Priya Shah: Are there limitations around GPU types in particular regions? We want A100s for some heavy models.
[05:49] Tess Nguyen: GPU availability varies by region; for example A100 and H100 availability differs across cloud regions. For Private we can provision nodes in regions that have the hardware you need, otherwise we discuss model/quantization tradeoffs.
[05:59] Mark Donnelly: Quick note — our mobile app does batching at the edge, so request sizes will be spiky. We need to understand autoscaling and warmup for KV cache.
[06:08] Miguel Ortega: KV cache warmup is real — we recommend warm pools and a pre-warming plan. Autoscaling policies can be configured by token throughput or concurrency; we can share sample policies.
[06:18] Priya Shah: Great. Can you also provide an example network diagram of the recommended setup for both TGW and PrivateLink?
[06:24] Sara Kim: Absolutely. We'll share a runbook that has diagrams: 1) Redwood in your account with interface endpoints, 2) Redwood in Redwood account with VPC peering, 3) TGW-based central model.
[06:35] Mark Donnelly: Next steps — we'd like to schedule a network deep-dive with our infra team. Also, can you do a small perf run with synthetic traces to show p95?
[06:44] Miguel Ortega: Yes, we'll prepare a benchmark plan. Need your sample request distribution and CIDR ranges to craft realistic tests.
[06:52] Priya Shah: I'll share. Also any compliance add-ons like increased log retention?
[06:56] Tess Nguyen: We have log retention add-ons and longer-term storage options; we'll include pricing in the follow-up.
[07:03] Sara Kim: Recap: Miguel will prepare benchmark plan. I'll send SOC2/docs and the network runbook. Priya will send CIDRs and region constraints. We'll aim to schedule the deep-dive the week of 7/6.
[07:15] Priya Shah: Sounds good. Thanks all.
[07:18] Mark Donnelly: Thanks.
[07:19] End of recording.
